name: Observer-expectancy effect
statement: An observer who knows which result is expected tends to obtain it, by cueing the subject or by scoring ambiguous evidence in the expected direction.
meaning: Two mechanisms travel under one name. An observer can change the subject's behaviour through posture, timing and the small signals any interaction carries. An observer can also change the record, marking a borderline case as a success because success is what the treatment should produce. Neither requires dishonesty and neither is available to introspection. This is the only bias in the atlas whose main product is a procedure rather than a finding: the rule that whoever measures an outcome should not know which condition produced it.

origin.where: the book Clever Hans (The Horse of Mr. von Osten), translated by Carl L. Rahn and published by Henry Holt
origin.note: The investigation came first. A commission convened by Carl Stumpf reported on 12 September 1904 that no regular signalling could be detected, and Pfungst published his own report on 9 December 1904. The German book preceded Rahn's English translation. The term experimenter expectancy belongs to Robert Rosenthal's programme of the 1960s, which extended the idea from a horse to human research participants.

evidence: Wilhelm von Osten's horse appeared to do arithmetic, spell, read the clock and name musical intervals by tapping a forefoot. Pfungst separated the two things nobody had separated: whether the horse knew the answer, and whether the questioner did. Asked to tap numerals on cards that nobody present could see, Hans was right in 8 percent of 49 tests; when the questioner could see the card, he was right in 98 percent of 42 tests. Across all the series, procedure with knowledge produced 90 to 100 percent correct answers and procedure without knowledge produced at most 10 percent. Blinders settled the channel. In 102 tests with large blinders the questioner was certainly out of sight in 35, seen in 56 and undecided in 11, and Hans scored 6 percent, 89 percent and 18 percent. The cue was a slight forward bend of the questioner's head and trunk, which started the tapping, and a slight upward jerk, which stopped it. Pfungst reproduced it deliberately: of thirty tests in which he simply stooped, twenty-nine set the horse tapping, and it kept tapping until he straightened up. He then reversed the roles and played the horse himself, reading twelve human subjects who were thinking of a word or a number, and averaging 73 percent correct over 350 tests. Rosenthal and Fode's 1963 rat study is the usual citation for the laboratory version of this. Its text is paywalled, so no figure from it appears on this page.

replication.headline: Where the same outcome in the same trial is judged by a blinded and a non-blinded assessor, the non-blinded one reports a bigger treatment effect, in study after study.
replication.detail: The clean design compares two assessors inside one trial, so the patients, the treatment and the randomisation are held fixed and only the assessor's knowledge varies. Hrobjartsson and colleagues found 21 such trials with binary outcomes covering 4,391 patients and pooled a ratio of odds ratios of 0.64 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.96), meaning non-blinded assessors exaggerated odds ratios by 36 percent. The two assessors agreed in a median of 78 percent of assessments, interquartile range 64 to 90 percent, and the whole distortion came from misclassifying a median of 3 percent of patients per trial. Salazar and colleagues updated the search to 2024 and reached 66 trials across 18 specialties, pooling 43 of them, 7,055 patients, at a ratio of odds ratios of 0.71 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.92), an exaggeration of 29 percent. The distortion ran larger in non-drug trials, 0.62 (0.46 to 0.84), and in industry-funded trials, 0.57 (0.37 to 0.88). The same design has been run on two other kinds of outcome. On subjective measurement scales, 16 trials covering 2,854 patients gave a pooled difference in effect size of minus 0.23 (95% CI minus 0.40 to minus 0.06), reported as an exaggeration of 68 percent (14 to 230 percent). On time-to-event outcomes, seven trials comparing an experimental intervention with a standard control gave a ratio of hazard ratios of 0.73 (0.57 to 0.93). Four cytomegalovirus retinitis trials in that review ran the other way, 1.33 (0.98 to 1.82), the non-blinded assessors favouring the control arm. Bello and colleagues took the design to animal experiments and pooled 10 experiments on 2,450 animals at a ratio of odds ratios of 0.41 (0.20 to 0.82). Three pesticide experiments carried that result, at 0.20 (0.07 to 0.59) against 0.82 (0.57 to 1.17) in the other seven. Outside medicine, Holman and colleagues matched 83 pairs of evolutionary biology studies on the same question, one blind and one not, and found the non-blind member of the pair reported the larger effect size in 53 of 83 pairs, 63 percent (95% CI 52 to 74 percent), an inflation of about 27 percent. In their text-mined sample of 12,710 papers, 13.4 percent were scored as blind. Other counts of how often field biologists work blind land in the same range. Kardish and colleagues read 492 articles in ecology, evolution and behaviour, judged 248 of them open to observer bias, and found blind observation stated in 33 of those 248, 13.3 percent, with no journal above 25 percent. Burghardt and colleagues sampled five animal behaviour journals across the 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000 and 2010 volumes and put blind scoring or inter-observer reliability under 10 percent, against over 80 percent in a journal on human infant behaviour. Freeberg, Benson and Burghardt repeated that count on the 2020 volumes of the same five journals and report a rise in all of them, still short of the infancy journal, with the figures behind a paywall. Holman's paper gives Burghardt's rate as 6.3 percent of 960 studies, quoted here from Holman rather than from Burghardt.

study.cite: Salazar, J., Moustgaard, H., Bracchiglione, J., & Hrobjartsson, A. (2025). Empirical evidence of observer bias in randomized clinical trials: updated and expanded analysis of trials with both blinded and non-blinded outcome assessors. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 183, 111787.

limits: The strongest counter-evidence is about blinding rather than about expectancy. The MetaBLIND study took the other comparison, between trials rather than within them, across 142 meta-analyses holding 1,153 trials. For lack of blinding of outcome assessors it found a ratio of odds ratios of 1.01 (95 percent credible interval 0.86 to 1.18) in 46 meta-analyses of subjective observer-reported outcomes, with no clear gradient by how subjective the outcome was, and no average difference for unblinded patients or clinicians either. Its authors offer two readings, that blinding matters less than believed or that the method is confounded, and recommend blinding anyway. A second limit is the kind of outcome. Wood and colleagues combined 146 meta-analyses holding 1,346 trials and found that lack of blinding exaggerated odds ratios for subjective outcomes, ratio of odds ratios 0.75 (95 percent CI 0.61 to 0.93), with no such sign for objective outcomes, 1.01 (0.92 to 1.10). Inside the subjective range no gradient appears either. Salazar's meta-regression found no association between the distortion and rated outcome subjectivity, P = 0.53, matching the null result Hrobjartsson's 2012 review got on the same question, P = 0.27. The trial figures come from medicine and from outcomes that require judgement, and they do not transfer untested to a psychology laboratory. Pfungst is one horse, one investigator and no statistics. Rosenthal's laboratory programme was contested at the time by Barber and Silver, whose 1968 monograph is named here from its Crossref record and read only through Bishop's summary of its argument, that the demonstrations rested on small samples and analytic flexibility. Rosenthal and Rubin's synthesis of 345 expectancy experiments is cited below for its design, which its abstract describes; the pooled magnitudes are in the body of a paywalled article and are not quoted here.
misreadings: The classroom study is treated as the demonstration and is the weakest link in the chain. Thorndike's review reprints Rosenthal and Jacobson's own table of first-year IQ gains: grade 1, 27.4 points for the 7 designated bloomers against 12.0 for 48 controls; grade 2, 16.5 for 12 against 7.0 for 47; then differences of 0.0, 3.4, minus 0.1 and minus 0.7 in grades 3 to 6. The whole effect rests on 19 children. Thorndike then went after the instrument and found a class of 19 pupils with a mean reasoning score of 31, a first-grade mean of 58, and six designated bloomers in one second-grade class with a post-test mean of 150.17 and a standard deviation of 40.17. Elashoff and Snow's reanalysis found no expectancy advantage in grades 3 to 6 and called grades 1 and 2 unresolvable, because the two groups differed so much at pre-test. Jussim and Harber's review answers the instrument attack rather than conceding it: an unreliable test adds noise, which makes a real difference harder to detect and not easier, so a bad instrument is a poor explanation for a difference that was found. The pygmalion-effect entry records both sides of that exchange. The second misreading is that knowing about the cue is enough to stop making it. Pfungst reported that the people he let in on the secret found it difficult and sometimes almost impossible to inhibit the movements on purpose. Blinding works by removing the observer's knowledge, not by asking for self-control. The third is confusion with the Hawthorne effect, which is about a subject who knows they are watched rather than an observer who knows what to expect.
